case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Rooker–Feldman doctrine bars a federal district court from hearing a plaintiff’s federal claims when the challenged state-court decision is not yet final because it remains subject to further review in the state appellate system.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1257 (exclusive Supreme Court review of final state-court judgments) and, by implication, 28 U.S.C. § 1331 (federal-question jurisdiction) as limited by the Rooker–Feldman doctrine.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: T.M. argues that Rooker–Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine tied to § 1257’s limitation to final state-court judgments, so it cannot be triggered by a non-final state-court decision still subject to state appellate review; accordingly, the federal district court had jurisdiction to hear her federal claims rather than dismissing them as an improper de facto appeal of state proceedings.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that T.M.’s federal suit is an impermissible attempt to obtain federal district-court review and rejection of a state-court consent order (i.e., a de facto appeal), and that the Rooker–Feldman requirements are satisfied on the facts as pleaded; they contend the doctrine can apply even while further state review may be available and that T.M’s complaint, in substance, seeks relief from the state-court judgment rather than presenting an independent federal claim.
key_precedents: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Thana v. Board of License Commissioners, 827 F.3d 314 (4th Cir. 2016)
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—functional finality and the risk of de facto appellate review—has force as a comity and case-management concern, but Exxon Mobil’s insistence that Rooker–Feldman applies only after “the state proceedings ended” counsels against converting that prudential worry into a jurisdictional rule. Justice Thomas’s § 1257 textual anchor is the most persuasive response: because § 1257 channels this Court’s review only of final state judgments, expanding Rooker–Feldman to interlocutory orders would untether the doctrine from its statutory premise and recreate the overbreadth Exxon Mobil rejected. Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh are right that abstention, stays, and preclusion can address parallel-proceedings friction without rewriting jurisdictional lines. A narrow holding that nonfinal state-court proceedings do not trigger Rooker–Feldman best preserves administrability and institutional legitimacy while leaving other doctrines available in appropriate cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the functional-finality/comity concern—that an interlocutory state order can be sufficiently operative that a federal suit becomes a de facto appeal—but that is a prudential objection, not a textual limitation on § 1331. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch both stress, Rooker–Feldman rests (if at all) on a negative implication from § 1257, and § 1257’s trigger is a “final” state judgment; expanding the jurisdictional bar to nonfinal orders untethers the doctrine from its only plausible statutory footing. Exxon Mobil’s “after the state proceedings ended” formulation confirms that finality is not optional, and the remaining interference concerns can be handled by abstention, stays, or preclusion rather than by rewriting Congress’s jurisdictional grants. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion identifies a contrary precedent that overcomes the original public meaning of § 1257’s final-judgment boundary.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains comity and the risk of de facto appellate review of ongoing state proceedings, but that is not a textual basis for converting Rooker–Feldman into an interlocutory jurisdictional bar. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Exxon Mobil repeatedly described the doctrine as confined to suits brought after “the state proceedings ended,” and treating nonfinal orders as “final enough” would expand what we have called an “exceptionally narrow” doctrine in a way untethered from § 1257’s final-judgment requirement. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on § 1257’s text reinforces that the negative implication at the heart of Rooker–Feldman makes sense only when there is a final state judgment of the kind reviewable here; absent that, the proper tools are abstention, stays, or (once final) preclusion. Practical consequences can matter, but they cannot justify rewriting a jurisdictional limit Congress did not enact.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains comity/functional-finality: an interlocutory state order can have immediate operative effects and a federal suit may look like a de facto appeal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Exxon Mobil’s limitation to suits brought after “the state proceedings ended” and § 1257’s final-judgment anchor make it illegitimate to convert those prudential worries into a categorical, jurisdictional bar. Justice Thomas’s textual point reinforces that expanding Rooker–Feldman beyond final state judgments would untether a narrow doctrine from its statutory footing and, in practice, close the federal courthouse to plaintiffs—often vulnerable—seeking to vindicate federal rights while state litigation is still ongoing. Comity can be protected through abstention, stays, and later preclusion, which are tailored tools that avoid the blunt, inequitable overreach Exxon Mobil cautioned against.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best shot is the functional-finality/comity point: that an interlocutory state order can be operative enough that a federal suit becomes a de facto appeal. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Exxon Mobil’s “after the state proceedings ended” limitation is doing real jurisdictional work, and Justice Thomas’s § 1257 anchor underscores why: Rooker–Feldman’s negative implication cannot sensibly extend to nonfinal orders still in the state appellate pipeline without recreating the overbreadth Exxon Mobil rejected. Workability and comity concerns are serious, but they are better handled through abstention, stays, and later preclusion, which are tailored and discretionary rather than a categorical stripping of § 1331 jurisdiction. On a pragmatic textualist approach, keeping the doctrine tied to statutory finality yields a clearer, more coherent rule and avoids turning “final enough” into an administrability mess.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains the “functional finality” concern—that an operative interlocutory state order can still make the federal suit look like a de facto appeal—but that is a comity/case-management problem, not a jurisdictional one. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Exxon Mobil’s limitation to cases brought after “the state proceedings ended” tracks § 1257’s textual requirement of a final state-court judgment, and we should not treat “final enough” as a substitute for finality without untethering the doctrine from its statutory mooring. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on § 1257 reinforces that Rooker–Feldman is (at most) a negative implication from Congress’s channeling of review of final state judgments to this Court; extending it to nonfinal orders would rewrite the jurisdictional lines Congress drew. Where parallel proceedings raise real friction, abstention, stays, and later preclusion provide tailored, nonjurisdictional tools without expanding an already narrow doctrine.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The best respondent argument remains functional finality and comity—warning that allowing § 1331 suits mid-stream invites de facto district-court review and forum shopping—but that concern is prudential and better addressed through abstention, stays, and ultimately preclusion, not by enlarging a jurisdictional bar. Chief Justice Roberts’s point that Rooker–Feldman is a negative implication from § 1257, which by its terms is limited to final state-court judgments, underscores that treating interlocutory orders as “final enough” would detach the doctrine from its statutory and historical footing. Justice Thomas’s textual emphasis reinforces that Exxon Mobil’s “after the state proceedings ended” limitation is not optional language but the administrable boundary that preserves the Court’s repeated insistence that Rooker–Feldman is “exceptionally narrow.” On an institutionalist approach, keeping the doctrine tethered to finality maintains predictable jurisdictional lines and avoids reviving the pre-Exxon overbreadth that undermines the Court’s legitimacy.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains the “functional finality” concern—that an interlocutory state order can operate like a final judgment and a federal suit would therefore resemble an appeal—but that argument does not square with § 1257’s text limiting this Court’s review to “final judgments” and Exxon Mobil’s requirement that Rooker–Feldman applies only after “the state proceedings ended.” Chief Justice Roberts persuasively explains that comity and administrability anxieties are real yet properly addressed through abstention, stays, and preclusion rather than by expanding a jurisdictional bar beyond its statutory mooring. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on § 1257’s finality anchor underscores that treating nonfinal orders as “final enough” would untether a narrow negative implication from Congress’s chosen jurisdictional boundary and improperly constrict § 1331. No colleague identified precedent compelling the functional-finality expansion, so my vote remains with petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the functional-finality/comity concern—that district court litigation during a pending state appeal can resemble de facto appellate review and create friction with state courts—but that is a problem for tailored, nonjurisdictional tools, not for expanding a judge-made jurisdictional bar beyond its statutory anchor. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Exxon Mobil’s limitation to suits filed after “the state proceedings ended” tracks the practical consequence I worry about: an interlocutory state ruling should not automatically slam the federal courthouse doors on independent federal claims, particularly where plaintiffs have no realistic federal forum otherwise. Justice Thomas’s § 1257 final-judgment emphasis underscores that Rooker–Feldman’s legitimacy depends on finality; absent a final state judgment, calling an order “rendered” for RF purposes looks like an untethered, administratively messy expansion. Because no colleague identified a precedent compelling the treatment of nonfinal state orders as “final enough,” my vote stays with petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rooker–Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s channeling of review of final state-court judgments to this Court, and Exxon Mobil confines it to suits by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced” and after “the state proceedings ended.” 544 U.S. at 284, 291. Where the challenged state-court decision remains subject to further review in the state appellate system, treating it as sufficiently “final” for Rooker–Feldman would expand the doctrine beyond Exxon Mobil’s limits and risk needless jurisdictional dismissals that can be handled, if appropriate, by preclusion or abstention principles rather than jurisdictional foreclosure. A narrow holding that nonfinal state proceedings do not trigger Rooker–Feldman best preserves institutional legitimacy by keeping the doctrine aligned with § 1257 while leaving other doctrines to address duplicative or interfering litigation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of 28 U.S.C. § 1257 limit this Court’s appellate review to “final” state-court judgments, and the Rooker–Feldman doctrine is a judge-made negative inference from that statute; it therefore should not be expanded to bar district-court jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 when the challenged state-court decision remains nonfinal and subject to further state appellate review. Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp. cabined Rooker–Feldman to suits brought by state-court losers “after the state proceedings ended,” complaining of injury caused by the state-court judgment and seeking its review and rejection, which presupposes finality consistent with § 1257. Extending the doctrine to interlocutory or otherwise nonfinal state orders would depart from the original, limited jurisdictional boundary reflected in § 1257 and improperly displace ordinary doctrines (preclusion, abstention) Congress has not made jurisdictional. Accordingly, the district court retained jurisdiction to hear independent federal claims while state appellate processes remained available.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Rooker–Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s channeling of review of final state-court judgments to this Court, and Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp. limits it to cases brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state judgments rendered before the federal suit and after the state proceedings have ended. Where the challenged state-court decision remains subject to further review in the state appellate system, it is not the kind of final judgment contemplated by § 1257, and extending Rooker–Feldman to such interlocutory situations would improperly expand a doctrine this Court has repeatedly characterized as “exceptionally narrow.” Practical consequences also counsel against expansion: ordinary doctrines like abstention and preclusion can protect state interests and prevent duplicative litigation without converting § 1257 into a broad bar on § 1331 jurisdiction. Accordingly, the district court should not dismiss for lack of jurisdiction under Rooker–Feldman solely because a non-final state order exists.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Rooker–Feldman is a narrow jurisdictional doctrine rooted in 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s assignment of exclusive Supreme Court review over final state-court judgments, and it should not be expanded to bar federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 when the challenged state-court decision remains nonfinal and subject to further state appellate review. Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp. confines the doctrine to suits by state-court losers brought after state proceedings have ended, complaining of injuries caused by the state-court judgment and inviting federal district-court review and rejection of that judgment. Treating nonfinal state proceedings as sufficient to trigger Rooker–Feldman would resurrect the “mischief” Exxon Mobil sought to prevent—needlessly shutting the federal courthouse doors to plaintiffs, including vulnerable litigants seeking to vindicate federal rights, even though ordinary doctrines like preclusion, abstention, or comity can address overlap with ongoing state processes. Because § 1257’s finality requirement is not satisfied, dismissal for lack of jurisdiction under Rooker–Feldman is unwarranted here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rooker–Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s assignment to this Court of exclusive review of final state-court judgments, and Exxon Mobil confines it to suits complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced.” 544 U.S. at 284. Reading “rendered” in light of § 1257’s final-judgment requirement, the doctrine should not bar federal-question jurisdiction under § 1331 when the challenged state-court decision remains subject to further state appellate review. Other doctrines—preclusion, abstention, or stays—can address comity and workability concerns without expanding a jurisdictional bar beyond its statutory foundation. Extending Rooker–Feldman to nonfinal state orders would create administrability problems and unsettle Exxon Mobil’s effort to keep the doctrine cabined.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rooker–Feldman is a narrow jurisdictional limitation rooted in 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s assignment of appellate review of state-court judgments to this Court, and § 1257 by its terms concerns review of final state-court judgments. Under Exxon Mobil, the doctrine is confined to suits by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced” and inviting federal district-court review and rejection of those judgments; a state-court decision still subject to state appellate review is not yet the kind of final judgment § 1257 contemplates. Extending Rooker–Feldman to nonfinal state rulings would depart from the statute’s text and the Court’s admonition against expanding the doctrine beyond Rooker and Feldman, while ordinary doctrines (preclusion, abstention where applicable) remain available to manage parallel proceedings without rewriting jurisdictional limits. Accordingly, the district court retained § 1331 jurisdiction over petitioner’s federal claims, and Rooker–Feldman should not bar them on the sole ground that an interlocutory state order exists.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Rooker–Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine rooted in 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s channeling of review of final state-court judgments exclusively to this Court, and it should not be expanded beyond that historical and statutory foundation. In Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., the Court confined the doctrine to cases brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced” and after “the state proceedings ended,” language that strongly indicates finality is required. Where the challenged state-court decision remains subject to further state appellate review, ordinary doctrines such as preclusion or abstention—not a categorical jurisdictional bar—address comity and workability concerns while preserving Congress’s grant of federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331. Extending Rooker–Feldman to non-final state proceedings would invite the “mischief” Exxon Mobil sought to prevent by converting many parallel or interlocutory disputes into premature jurisdictional dismissals.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Rooker–Feldman is a narrow jurisdictional doctrine grounded in 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s assignment to this Court of exclusive review of final state-court judgments, and Exxon Mobil confines it to suits by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before” the federal action begins. A state-court order that remains subject to further review in the state appellate system is not a “final” judgment within § 1257’s logic, so applying Rooker–Feldman at that interlocutory stage would extend the doctrine beyond its statutory premise and beyond Exxon Mobil’s limiting formulation. To the extent respondents’ concerns sound in comity or duplication, those are addressed by doctrines like abstention or preclusion, not by expanding a jurisdictional bar beyond its textually and historically supported scope. Accordingly, the district court retained § 1331 jurisdiction over independent federal claims notwithstanding ongoing state appellate proceedings.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rooker–Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s channeling of federal appellate review of final state-court judgments to this Court, and it should not be expanded to bar § 1331 federal-question suits when the state-court decision remains nonfinal within the state appellate process. Exxon Mobil confines the doctrine to cases where the plaintiff complains of an injury caused by a state-court judgment “rendered before the district court proceedings commenced,” a formulation best read—consistent with § 1257’s text—to mean a final, operative judgment not subject to further state review. Treating nonfinal state orders as triggering Rooker–Feldman would unnecessarily strip federal courts of congressionally conferred jurisdiction and invite inequitable, practical consequences by forcing litigants to wait out state appellate timelines even when they raise independent federal claims. Any concerns about duplicative litigation or federal interference can be handled through abstention, preclusion, or comity doctrines rather than an overbroad jurisdictional bar.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars a federal district court from hearing a plaintiff’s federal claims when the challenged state-court decision is not final because it remains subject to further review in the state-court system.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1257 (Supreme Court review of final state-court judgments) as implemented through the judge-made Rooker-Feldman doctrine limiting lower federal courts’ jurisdiction; with background reliance on 28 U.S.C. § 1331 (federal question jurisdiction).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: T.M. argues that Rooker-Feldman is a narrow jurisdictional doctrine that applies only to final state-court judgments; because the Maryland consent order was still subject to further review in Maryland courts (and her state appeal had not been resolved), the federal suit should not be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. She also contends her federal action is an independent challenge (e.g., to the legality of her detention/commitment-related conduct) rather than an impermissible de facto appeal seeking federal review and rejection of a state-court judgment.
case_analysis.respondent_position: UMMS and the other respondents argue that Congress did not give federal district courts appellate authority over state-court judgments, and T.M.’s federal complaint is functionally an attempt to overturn or obtain relief from the state-court consent order governing her discharge. On that view, the injury she alleges is caused by the state-court judgment itself, and the relief requested would effectively negate it; therefore the district court lacked jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman even if state appellate proceedings were ongoing or the consent order was later challenged in state court.
key_precedents: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
Thana v. Board of License Commissioners for Charles County, Maryland, 827 F.3d 314 (4th Cir. 2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point—an interlocutory order can be practically operative and thus a functional “judgment,” so a federal suit risks de facto appellate review—has force as a comity concern, but it does not justify expanding a narrow, judge-made jurisdictional doctrine beyond Exxon Mobil’s finality- and posture-based limits. Justice Thomas’s anchoring in § 1257 finality is especially persuasive: if Congress channeled our review to final state judgments, lower-court jurisdiction should not be curtailed more broadly by implication. Justice Kagan’s workability warning also resonates under a minimalist approach; treating revisable orders as jurisdiction-stripping would sweep ordinary parallel-proceeding disputes into mandatory dismissals, when abstention, stays, and preclusion can address interference without rewriting § 1331. I therefore remain with petitioner and would favor a narrow holding: Rooker-Feldman does not apply absent a final state-court judgment in the Rooker/Feldman posture, leaving other doctrines to manage ongoing state proceedings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point—that an interlocutory consent order can be the operative source of injury and thus should be treated as a “judgment” for Rooker-Feldman—still fails under the doctrine’s only legitimate textual anchor: § 1257’s limitation to review of “final judgments.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Exxon Mobil confines Rooker-Feldman to the posture where state proceedings have ended and a judgment was rendered before the federal case began; expanding the doctrine to nonfinal, revisable orders would be an atextual contraction of § 1331 that Congress did not enact. The practical federalism/comity concerns respondents invoke are real, but, as Justice Alito notes, they are properly managed through abstention, stays, and preclusion—tools that restrain without jurisdiction-stripping. No colleague has identified a precedent undermining Exxon’s finality-centric limitation, so my vote remains for petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point remains the practical/comity concern that federal jurisdiction over claims intertwined with ongoing state proceedings can become de facto appellate supervision of state courts, particularly when an interlocutory order is the operative source of the plaintiff’s alleged injury. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas persuasively anchor Rooker-Feldman to § 1257’s channeling of review of final state judgments to this Court; extending the doctrine to nonfinal, still-reviewable orders would be an atextual expansion that improperly contracts Congress’s § 1331 grant and risks turning Rooker-Feldman into a broad, workability-poor abstention surrogate. The better, more practical way to protect state processes is through tailored tools—Younger/Colorado River abstention, stays, and preclusion—rather than a jurisdictional rule that sweeps in ordinary parallel-litigation situations. No colleague identified any precedent that genuinely dislodges Exxon Mobil’s finality-centric limitation, so I remain with petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point—that a nonfinal state order can be practically operative and thus a federal suit risks de facto appellate review—sounds in comity, but Exxon Mobil (as Justice Kagan emphasizes) deliberately confines Rooker-Feldman to the posture where state proceedings have ended and a judgment was rendered before the federal case in the § 1257-finality sense. Justice Thomas’s anchor in § 1257’s “final judgments” is especially persuasive to me because expanding a judge-made jurisdictional bar beyond the boundary that limits even our own review would disproportionately block federal-rights claims by people least able to endure prolonged state processes. If the federal complaint targets independent injuries attributable to defendants’ conduct rather than the state judgment itself, jurisdiction should lie under § 1331, with Younger/Colorado River, stays, and preclusion doing the tailoring work. That approach preserves access to a federal forum while still allowing district courts to avoid improper interference with ongoing state supervision through nonjurisdictional tools.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that an interlocutory state order can be the immediate source of a plaintiff’s injury, so a federal suit may look like de facto appellate review and risk interference with state processes. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Exxon Mobil ties Rooker-Feldman to the § 1257 channeling function over final state judgments and to the posture where state proceedings have ended; extending the doctrine to nonfinal, revisable orders would make it an unworkably broad, atextual contraction of § 1331 and largely redundant of abstention/preclusion. Even if the federal remedy would practically undermine a state order, that concern is better handled through Younger/Colorado River, stays, or ordinary preclusion—not by recharacterizing every operative interlocutory directive as a “judgment” that strips jurisdiction. No colleague has identified a precedent that plausibly dislodges Exxon’s finality-centric boundary, so my vote remains for petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondents’ best point—that interlocutory state orders can operate like judgments and federal review would undermine comity—sounds more in abstention than in jurisdiction. Justice Thomas’s reliance on § 1257’s “final judgments” limitation and the negative-implication logic is the only plausible textual anchor for Rooker-Feldman, and it cuts against extending a judge-made, jurisdiction-stripping doctrine to nonfinal, still-reviewable state orders. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Exxon Mobil deliberately confined Rooker-Feldman to the posture where state proceedings have ended and a judgment was rendered before the federal suit; any broader rule would atextually contract § 1331 and invite courts to police comity through an ill-fitting jurisdictional label. Concerns about end-runs and interference can be handled through Younger/Colorado River, stays, and preclusion without rewriting Congress’s jurisdictional scheme.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point remains the comity/workaround concern: a federal challenge to an interlocutory state order can look like de facto appellate review and invite end-runs around state supervision. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s arguments persuade me that Exxon Mobil ties Rooker-Feldman to the § 1257 final-judgment framework and the classic posture where state proceedings have ended; extending the doctrine to nonfinal, still-reviewable orders would be an atextual expansion of a narrow, judge-made jurisdictional bar and would unduly contract § 1331. Justice Barrett’s workability point reinforces that ordinary parallel-proceedings problems should be handled through abstention, stays, or preclusion rather than by recharacterizing interlocutory orders as “final judgments” for jurisdictional purposes. On an institutionalist view, keeping Rooker-Feldman confined to its historical and statutory anchor better preserves coherence, administrability, and the Court’s legitimacy than broadening it to police comity concerns indirectly.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point remains that an interlocutory state order can be immediately operative and that a federal suit seeking to negate it looks like de facto appellate review, but Exxon Mobil’s limiting formulation—emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan—ties Rooker-Feldman to the Rooker/Feldman posture where state proceedings have ended and a judgment was rendered before the federal case began. Justice Thomas’s § 1257 anchor is decisive under a textualist lens: because Congress confined this Court’s review-channeling to “final judgments,” it is difficult to justify a broader, judge-made jurisdictional withdrawal for lower courts that sweeps in nonfinal, revisable orders. Treating interlocutory orders as jurisdiction-stripping would also collapse Rooker-Feldman into an atextual, workability-eroding substitute for abstention and preclusion, which are the proper tools for managing comity and parallel litigation. Nothing in the colleagues’ discussion identifies precedent warranting departure from Exxon’s finality-centric boundary, so I remain with petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point—that an operative, even if interlocutory, consent order can function like a “judgment” whose negation the federal plaintiff effectively seeks—raises real comity and interference concerns, but it does not justify converting those concerns into a categorical jurisdictional bar. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s anchoring of Rooker-Feldman to § 1257 finality, as reinforced by Exxon Mobil’s limitation to cases where state proceedings have ended and a judgment was rendered before the federal suit, makes clear that stretching the doctrine to revisitable orders would be an atextual expansion that improperly contracts § 1331. Justice Kagan’s workability point is decisive for me as a pragmatic matter: using abstention, stays, and preclusion to manage overlap is more tailored and procedurally fair than dismissing for lack of jurisdiction whenever a nonfinal state order is implicated. Thus, any “de facto appeal” worry here goes to merits or equitable restraint, not to stripping the district court of subject-matter jurisdiction.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rooker-Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s channeling of review of final state-court judgments to this Court, and Exxon Mobil confined it to cases where the state-court loser complains of an injury caused by a state-court judgment “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced” in circumstances akin to Rooker and Feldman—i.e., after the state proceedings have ended. Where the challenged state-court order remains subject to further review within the state system, treating it as a conclusive “judgment” for Rooker-Feldman purposes would expand the doctrine beyond Exxon Mobil and risk unnecessary foreclosure of federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331. Any remaining concerns about parallel litigation, comity, and federalism can be handled through ordinary doctrines (preclusion, abstention, or stays) rather than a broad jurisdictional bar. A narrow holding that Rooker-Feldman does not apply absent a final state-court judgment best preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to precedent and avoiding unwarranted jurisdictional contraction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution and Congress have limited this Court’s review of state-court judgments to "[f]inal judgments" under 28 U.S.C. § 1257, and the judge-made Rooker-Feldman doctrine is at most a narrow negative implication from that text that prevents lower federal courts from exercising de facto appellate review of such final state judgments. Under Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005), Rooker-Feldman applies only in the limited circumstance where a state-court loser, after the state proceedings have ended, sues in federal district court complaining of an injury caused by the state-court judgment and seeking its review and rejection. Because the challenged Maryland consent order remained subject to further review within the state system, § 1257’s finality prerequisite is not met, and extending Rooker-Feldman here would improperly curtail Congress’ grant of federal-question jurisdiction in 28 U.S.C. § 1331. Any overlap between the federal claims and the state proceedings should be addressed through ordinary preclusion and abstention principles, not an overbroad jurisdictional bar untethered from § 1257’s text and original meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Rooker-Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine grounded in 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s assignment of review of final state-court judgments to this Court, not to federal district courts. Under Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., it applies only when a state-court loser files in federal court after the state proceedings have ended, complaining of injuries caused by the state-court judgment and seeking review and rejection of that judgment; where state proceedings remain ongoing and the challenged order is still subject to state-court review, that jurisdictional bar is not triggered. The respondents’ concerns about interference with state processes can be addressed through other doctrines (e.g., preclusion or abstention) rather than expanding Rooker-Feldman beyond its textual anchor in finality under § 1257. Limiting Rooker-Feldman to final judgments respects Congress’s jurisdictional scheme while avoiding unnecessary dismissal of federal-question claims within § 1331.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Rooker-Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine rooted in 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s limitation of Supreme Court review to final state-court judgments, and Exxon Mobil confines it to cases where the state-court judgment was “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced.” 544 U.S. at 284. Where the challenged state-court decision remains subject to further review in the state system, treating it as “final” for Rooker-Feldman would improperly expand the doctrine and deny a federal forum for independent federal claims within 28 U.S.C. § 1331. Properly understood, disputes about overlap with ongoing state proceedings are better managed through abstention, preclusion, or comity doctrines—not by converting Rooker-Feldman into a broad bar that forecloses access to federal court for vulnerable plaintiffs alleging federal-rights violations. Because the decision is not final and petitioner plausibly alleges injuries from defendants’ conduct rather than solely from the judgment itself, the district court retains jurisdiction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rooker-Feldman is a narrow, judge-made limit derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s channeling of review of final state-court judgments to this Court, and Exxon Mobil confines it to suits complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced” and seeking federal-court “review and rejection” of those judgments. 544 U.S. at 284, 291–92. Where the challenged state-court decision is not final because it remains subject to further state-court review, applying Rooker-Feldman would overread § 1257 and create an unworkable, overbroad jurisdictional bar inconsistent with Exxon’s timing/finality emphasis and its insistence that parallel or ongoing state proceedings do not themselves strip § 1331 jurisdiction. Other doctrines (preclusion, abstention, stays) can manage comity and duplication without transforming Rooker-Feldman into a sweeping nonfinality rule that blocks federal claims categorically.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rooker-Feldman is a narrow, judge-made limit on lower federal courts’ jurisdiction derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s assignment to this Court of review of final state-court judgments, and Exxon Mobil confines it to suits by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced” and inviting review and rejection of those judgments. Where the challenged state-court order remains subject to further state-court review and thus is not final for § 1257 purposes, extending Rooker-Feldman would expand atextual jurisdictional limits beyond Congress’s scheme and wrongly displace the ordinary tools for handling parallel litigation (preclusion, abstention, comity) rather than denying § 1331 jurisdiction. On this understanding, the district court retains jurisdiction to hear independent federal claims, even if related to ongoing state proceedings, so long as it is not exercising de facto appellate review of a final state judgment. Limiting the doctrine to final judgments respects separation of powers by hewing to the jurisdiction Congress actually specified in §§ 1257 and 1331 and avoids the “mischief” Exxon Mobil sought to end.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Rooker-Feldman is a narrow, jurisdictional doctrine tied to 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s channeling of review of final state-court judgments to this Court, and Exxon Mobil confines it to suits brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced” and inviting review and rejection of those judgments. Where the challenged state-court decision remains subject to further review in the state system, treating it as “final” for Rooker-Feldman purposes would expand the doctrine beyond Exxon Mobil and create practical, workability problems by converting many parallel or ongoing state proceedings into federal jurisdictional bars rather than addressing them through ordinary doctrines like preclusion or abstention. Consistent with Exxon Mobil and the history of § 1257, the district court retains § 1331 jurisdiction over independent federal claims so long as the plaintiff is not seeking de facto appellate review of a final state-court judgment. The better course for institutional legitimacy and judicial restraint is to keep Rooker-Feldman limited and leave any overlap with ongoing state proceedings to non-jurisdictional doctrines.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Rooker-Feldman is a judge-made gloss on 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s channeling of review of final state-court judgments to this Court, and it therefore should not be extended to bar federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 when the relevant state proceedings have not ended and remain subject to further state-court review. Exxon Mobil confines the doctrine to suits by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments rendered before the federal action is filed, emphasizing that the doctrine is “narrow” and keyed to the posture in Rooker and Feldman—where state proceedings had concluded. Where a plaintiff brings federal claims while state appellate review is ongoing, ordinary doctrines (preclusion, abstention) can address overlap without converting interlocutory state orders into jurisdiction-stripping “final judgments.” Extending Rooker-Feldman to nonfinal state decisions would untether the doctrine from § 1257’s text and distort the careful limits articulated in Exxon Mobil.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rooker-Feldman is a narrow, judge-made jurisdictional limitation rooted in 28 U.S.C. § 1257’s reservation of Supreme Court review for final state-court judgments, and Exxon Mobil confines it to suits by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments “rendered before the federal district court proceedings commenced” and inviting review and rejection of those judgments. Because the challenged Maryland consent order was not final—remaining subject to further review in the state system—treating it as a “judgment rendered before” would improperly expand Rooker-Feldman beyond § 1257’s finality premise and create needless jurisdictional dismissals that impede vindication of federal rights authorized by 28 U.S.C. § 1331. Any overlap with ongoing state proceedings is better handled through preclusion, abstention doctrines, or case-management tools, rather than a categorical jurisdictional bar. On this record, the federal claims can be understood as independent challenges to alleged unlawful conduct surrounding detention/commitment rather than a de facto appeal of a final state-court judgment, so the district court should not be stripped of jurisdiction.
